slides.title: What is a sensor?
points: A sensor detects a physical, chemical or biological change and converts it into a measurable signal.
slides.say: Use temperature, glucose and gas sensors as quick examples.
slides.ask: Ask students to identify input, sensing element, signal and output.

slides.title: Why sensors matter in smart systems
points: Glucose and wearable sensors track body chemistry.
Gas sensors detect air pollutants such as NOx and SOx.
Sensors help maintain concentration, pH and process safety.
Colorimetric methods help estimate copper in PCB samples.
slides.say: Ask students where sensors appear in a phone or lab.

slides.title: What is colorimetry?

slides.title: Electrochemical gas sensors

slides.title: What is corrosion?

definition.text: Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a metal by chemical or electrochemical reaction with its environment.

slides.say: Connect corrosion to rusting and electronic-device failure.

slides.title: Differential metal corrosion

definition.text: Differential metal corrosion occurs when two dissimilar metals are electrically connected in an electrolyte; the more active metal becomes anodic and corrodes.

slides.say: Use steel-copper contact as an example.
slides.ask: Ask students to identify input, sensing element, signal and output.

slides.title: Differential aeration corrosion

definition.text: Differential aeration corrosion occurs when different areas of a metal surface receive different oxygen concentrations, creating anodic and cathodic regions.

slides.say: Stress low oxygen area usually becomes anodic.
slides.ask: Ask students to identify input, sensing element, signal and output.

slides.title: Waterline corrosion

definition.text: Waterline corrosion is differential aeration corrosion near the water-air boundary, where oxygen concentration differs above and below the waterline.

slides.say: Use ship hulls/tanks as examples.
slides.ask: Ask students to identify input, sensing element, signal and output.

slides.title: Pitting corrosion

definition.text: Pitting corrosion is highly localized corrosion that forms small holes or pits, often when a protective film breaks down locally.

slides.say: Explain pits are dangerous because they look small but penetrate deeply.

slides.title: Galvanization

definition.text: Galvanization protects iron or steel by coating it with zinc, which provides barrier protection and sacrificial protection.

slides.title: Anodization

definition.text: Anodization is an electrochemical process that thickens the natural oxide layer on a metal surface, especially aluminium, to improve corrosion resistance.

slides.title: Vapour corrosion inhibitors

definition.text: Vapour corrosion inhibitors are volatile chemicals that vaporize, reach metal surfaces and form a protective adsorbed film against corrosion.

slides.title: Corrosion penetration rate
points: Corrosion penetration rate expresses how fast corrosion penetrates into a metal surface, usually as thickness loss per unit time.
slides.say: Tell students CPR converts lab weight loss into practical damage rate.
slides.ask: Ask students to identify input, sensing element, signal and output.

slides.title: CPR formula and units

definition.text: CPR = K W / (D A T) W = weight loss D = density A = exposed area T = exposure time K = unit constant

points: Exam method: write the equation, define symbols, substitute values with units, and state the practical meaning of the result.
slides.say: Define each symbol clearly before substituting values.

slides.title: Worked CPR template

definition.text: Given: W, D, A, T CPR = K W / (D A T) If W increases or area/time decreases, CPR becomes larger. Interpret: higher CPR means faster metal loss.

points: Exam method: write the equation, define symbols, substitute values with units, and state the practical meaning of the result.
